Q: How to use Pylint or other linters with Jupyter Notebooks? A:

You can use the Ruff linter, which natively supports Python in Jupyter Notebooks.

If you'd like, you can also use the Pylint rules exclusively with a similar output format by adding this to pyproject.toml:

[tool.ruff]
output-format = "pylint"

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["PL"]

Q: Google Sheets COUNTIF wont read output of IMPORTRANGE A:

May be there are data type mismatch ? like text string type and Boolean types? If so then Try wrapping your criteria in quotation marks so COUNTIF looks for the text string "TRUE". Like this ,
=COUNTIF(A:A, "TRUE")

Q: Morse code translating morse into language java A:

One thing that trips people up with Morse-to-text is handling the spacing correctly. Each letter is separated by a single space, and each word is separated by three spaces (or a forward slash in some implementations). If your HashMap lookup is failing, double-check that you're splitting on the right delimiter first — that's usually the root cause in Java implementations like this.

Q: What do fgetc and fputc have to do that using fread or fwrite on a big block avoids A:

3 thoughts:

Push back:

C allows ungetc() of at least 1 character so fgetc() needs to check for the push-back character each time it is called. fread() may only need to do this for the first character, thus simplifies the reading of subsequent characters.

Parameter checking, set up and I/O access locking

Each function incurs some O(1) overhead per call. Thus n calls to fgetc()/fputc() incur n times this overhead, fread()/fwrite() incurs 1 times this overhead, even when n is large.

Error checking:

Somewhat like the above. Each completed I/O function may generate an I/O error or end-of-file (on reads). This is done n times when calling single character functions, yet usual is done once on fread(n)/fwrite(n).
